title: Soviet Caucasus
subtitle: 1953–1991 · The Thaw, Stagnation and the Republics' National Movements, Karabakh, the Earthquake and Independence

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Mzhavanadze, Shevardnadze and Patiashvili, Demirchyan and Aliyev, the republics' leaders under Brezhnev and Gorbachev, and the new presidents of 1991

entries.label: Mzhavanadze and Shevardnadze in Georgia
entries.hint: Vasil Mzhavanadze (first secretary 1953–1972), who presided over a period of relative cultural latitude and corruption, was replaced by Eduard Shevardnadze, a former interior minister who led an anti-corruption campaign from 1972 and a Georgia of the shadow economy until 1985, when he became Soviet foreign minister.
entries.note: Ronald Suny, The Making of the Georgian Nation (1994); Eduard Shevardnadze, The Future Belongs to Freedom (1991).

entries.label: Heydar Aliyev in Azerbaijan
entries.hint: Heydar Aliyev, a former KGB general, was first secretary of the Azerbaijani party from 1969 to 1982, then a full member of the Politburo and first deputy prime minister of the USSR until forced out by Gorbachev in October 1987; he promoted Azerbaijani cadres, built a base in the republic and returned to power in 1993.
entries.note: Audrey Altstadt, The Azerbaijani Turks (1992); Tadeusz Swietochowski, Russia and Azerbaijan (1995).

entries.label: Demirchyan in Armenia
entries.hint: Karen Demirchyan, first secretary of the Armenian party from 1974 to 1988, a technocrat who built up industry, housing and culture and was popular, was removed in May 1988 after the first months of the Karabakh crisis and the Sumgait events.
entries.note: Ronald Suny, Looking toward Ararat (1993); Richard Hovannisian (ed.), The Armenian People, vol. 2 (1997).

entries.label: Gorbachev's reforms in the republics
entries.hint: Perestroika and glasnost, launched in 1985, brought the growth of independent associations and national fronts in the republics, the rise of the Armenian National Movement under Levon Ter-Petrosyan, the Azerbaijani Popular Front under Abulfaz Elchibey and the Georgian movements of Gamsakhurdia, Chanturia and Gachechiladze, and the end of party monopoly.

entries.label: Gamsakhurdia, Ter-Petrosyan and Mutalibov
entries.hint: In the first multiparty elections of October 1990 the nationalist bloc of Zviad Gamsakhurdia won a majority in Georgia, in the Armenian elections of 1990 the Armenian National Movement under Levon Ter-Petrosyan took the leading seat and in August 1990 he became chairman of the Supreme Council, and in Azerbaijan the Communist Ayaz Mutalibov became president in 1990 and was confirmed in a popular vote in September 1991; Gamsakhurdia was elected Georgia's president on 26 May 1991.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Tbilisi shooting of 1956, Sumgait, the Karabakh war's beginning, Tbilisi 1989, Baku in January 1990 and the first armed conflicts in Abkhazia and South Ossetia

entries.label: The Tbilisi demonstrations of March 1956
entries.hint: After Khrushchev's secret speech of February 1956 condemned Stalin, Georgian students and crowds gathered in Tbilisi on 5 March, the third anniversary of Stalin's death, to defend his memory and some, with nationalist slogans, demanded measures including a telegram to Molotov; Soviet troops fired on the crowd on the night of 9 March, killing, by official account, 21 people and by others more, many scores.
entries.note: Suny 1994; Georgian archival and memoir accounts.

entries.label: The language protest of 1978
entries.hint: When a draft Georgian constitution of 1978 dropped the clause that made Georgian the state language, thousands of students and others marched to the government house on 14 April 1978 and Shevardnadze, who gave way, restored the text; it was the largest popular demonstration in Georgia since 1956 and was the first success of a mass movement.
entries.note: Constitution of the Georgian SSR (1978); Suny 1994.

entries.label: The Karabakh movement
entries.hint: In February 1988 mass demonstrations began in Stepanakert and in Yerevan, with hundreds of thousands on Theatre Square, in support of the transfer of the Nagorno-Karabakh autonomous oblast from Azerbaijan to Armenia; on 20 February the oblast soviet voted for the transfer. Armenians cited the majority of Armenians in the oblast (some three-quarters), history and cultural repression; Azerbaijanis cited the borders and territorial integrity and economic ties; Moscow refused.
entries.note: Resolutions of the NKAO soviet (20 February 1988, 12 July 1988); Suny 1993; Altstadt 1992; Thomas de Waal, Black Garden (2003).

entries.label: Sumgait
entries.hint: In three days of February 1988 mobs attacked the Armenian inhabitants of the industrial city of Sumgait, killing, according to the official count, 26 Armenians and 6 Azerbaijanis, with rapes, burning and looting, and a delay in the arrival of Soviet troops; Armenian accounts give a larger number and speak of an organised pogrom, and the events led to the flight of Armenians from Azerbaijan and to the radicalisation of the Karabakh issue.
entries.note: Soviet prosecutor's reports; Suny 1993; de Waal 2003; Svante Cornell, Small Nations and Great Powers (2001).

entries.label: Kirovabad, Baku and Armenian villages
entries.hint: In November 1988 disturbances in Kirovabad (Ganja) and the expulsion of Azerbaijani villagers from Armenia in 1988–1989 were followed in January 1990 by a pogrom of Armenians in Baku, in which dozens of Armenians were killed during several days, by some counts about 90; some 350,000 Armenians left Azerbaijan and some 170,000 to 200,000 Azerbaijanis left Armenia between 1988 and 1990, in a population exchange made by force.
entries.note: Memorial and Helsinki Watch reports (1990–1992); de Waal 2003; Hovannisian 1997.

entries.label: Tbilisi, 9 April 1989
entries.hint: In the early hours of 9 April 1989 Soviet troops, with sapper spades and toxic gas, cleared a peaceful rally outside the government house in Rustaveli Avenue, which had been demanding independence from the USSR and protesting against Abkhaz secessionist demands; twenty-one people, mostly young women, were killed and hundreds injured. The act was a turning point for Georgian opinion; 9 April is a national day.
entries.note: Inquiry of the Sobchak Commission (1989); Suny 1994.

entries.label: Sukhumi, July 1989 and the first conflict in Abkhazia
entries.hint: In March 1989 some 30,000 Abkhaz at Lykhny demanded secession from Georgia and a separate republic; on 15–16 July riots between Georgians and Abkhaz followed the opening of a branch of Tbilisi University in Sukhumi, in which a number of people were killed, and the clashes deepened the divide that would lead to the war of 1992–1993.
entries.note: Soviet inquiry; Suny 1994; Svante Cornell, Autonomy and Conflict (2002).

entries.label: South Ossetia and the abolition of the oblast
entries.hint: In November 1989 clashes between Georgians and Ossetians broke out around Tskhinvali, as the South Ossetian popular front sought union with North Ossetia in Russia; on 11 December 1990 the Georgian parliament abolished the South Ossetian autonomous oblast, and in January 1991 fighting began with Georgian forces entering Tskhinvali, leading to a war and thousands of refugees; each side blames the other for its origin.
entries.note: Cornell 2002; Suny 1994; Human Rights Watch, Bloodshed in the Caucasus (1992).

entries.label: Black January
entries.hint: On the night of 19–20 January 1990, after the January pogrom of Armenians and the Popular Front's blockade of Soviet garrisons, 26,000 Soviet troops entered Baku, killing in the next days some 130 to 150 civilians, according to official count 131, with hundreds wounded, and the state of emergency was imposed; the date, 20 January, is a day of mourning in Azerbaijan, and the arrival of the army turned the Popular Front against Moscow.
entries.note: Human Rights Watch, Black January in Azerbaijan (1991); Altstadt 1992; de Waal 2003.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The 1978 language protests, the Karabakh resolutions, the sovereignty declarations and the independence acts of 1990–1991

entries.label: The Karabakh resolutions
entries.hint: The Nagorno-Karabakh oblast soviet voted on 20 February 1988 and again on 12 July 1988 to unite with Armenia; on 1 December 1989 the Supreme Council of Armenia and the oblast's soviet announced the 'reunification' of Karabakh with Armenia, to which Azerbaijan responded with a blockade; in January 1989 Moscow set up a special administration under Arkady Volsky, ended in November 1989.
entries.note: Resolutions of 20 February, 12 July and 1 December 1989; de Waal 2003.

entries.label: The acts of sovereignty
entries.hint: Azerbaijan's Supreme Soviet adopted a sovereignty law on 23 September 1989, which gave the republic the right of veto against the all-Union law; Armenia's Supreme Council adopted a Declaration of Independence on 23 August 1990, and Georgia's declared its sovereignty on 18 November 1989; the three states thus started their way out of the union.

entries.label: The independence acts of 1991
entries.hint: Georgia declared independence on 9 April 1991 after a referendum on 31 March (some 99 per cent in favour); Azerbaijan adopted the Constitutional Act on state independence on 18 October 1991; and Armenia's referendum of 21 September 1991 had about 99 per cent for independence, followed by a declaration on 23 September; the Soviet Union was dissolved by the Belovezha and Alma-Ata agreements in December.

entries.label: The Nagorno-Karabakh Republic
entries.hint: On 2 September 1991 the Armenian deputies of the oblast and of the Shahumyan district proclaimed the Nagorno-Karabakh Republic, and on 10 December 1991 a referendum, boycotted by the Azerbaijani population, found over 99 per cent for independence; Azerbaijan abolished the oblast's autonomy on 26 November 1991. The legal basis and the status of the state are contested.
entries.note: Declaration of 2 September 1991; Referendum of 10 December 1991; Azerbaijani law of 26 November 1991; de Waal 2003.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Vazgen I and Ilia II, the Muslim board at Baku and the revival of faith

entries.label: Vazgen I and Ilia II
entries.hint: The Armenian Catholicos Vazgen I (1955–1994) restored Etchmiadzin's authority, built links with the diaspora and was a figure of the commemoration of the genocide, which the demonstrations of 1965 had forced on the authorities, and the Georgian Catholicos-Patriarch Ilia II (from 1977) built up the Georgian church's moral position and public role; both institutions became symbols of the nations in the last Soviet years.

entries.label: The Spiritual Board of Transcaucasian Muslims
entries.hint: The Muslim Spiritual Board of Transcaucasia, based in Baku and headed from 1980 by Sheikh ul-Islam Allahshukur Pashazade, was the official body for Shia and Sunni Muslims of the Caucasus, with a few mosques and one madrasa; with glasnost, mosque openings and pilgrimages grew in 1989–1991.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Parajanov, Abuladze and the Matenadaran, the Genocide memorial and the mugham schools

entries.label: Mugham, Georgian song and sport
entries.hint: Azerbaijani composers such as Kara Karayev and Fikret Amirov, with the singers Rashid Behbudov and Muslim Magomayev, brought the mugham and Soviet pop to a wide audience; Georgian polyphonic choirs and the chess champion Nona Gaprindashvili, the footballers of Dinamo Tbilisi, winners of the Cup Winners' Cup in 1981, and Ararat Yerevan, Soviet champion in 1973, made the republics' names.

entries.label: The Genocide memorial and the Matenadaran
entries.hint: The Matenadaran, the institute of ancient manuscripts, was opened in 1957 as a repository of Armenia's manuscript heritage, and the memorial of Tsitsernakaberd to the victims of the genocide, designed by Arthur Tarkhanyan and Sashur Kalashyan, was completed in 1967 after the great demonstration of 24 April 1965.

entries.label: Parajanov and Abuladze
entries.hint: Sergei Parajanov, an Armenian film-maker born in Tbilisi, made 'The Colour of Pomegranates' (1969) on the poet Sayat-Nova and was imprisoned in 1973–1977; Tengiz Abuladze's 'Repentance' (1984), a parable of a dictator, was shown from 1986 and became the symbol of Georgian glasnost; Otar Iosseliani and Georgian cinema won international prizes.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The dissidents, the Armenian Committee of Karabakh and the Popular Front

entries.label: The dissidents and the national fronts
entries.hint: Georgian dissidents such as Zviad Gamsakhurdia and Merab Kostava, who were imprisoned in the 1970s, the Armenian National United Party of Paruyr Hayrikyan (1966), and the Karabakh Committee of Yerevan intellectuals (1988), among them Levon Ter-Petrosyan, Vazgen Manukyan and Ashot Manucharyan, formed the nuclei of the independence movements, and the Azerbaijani Popular Front of 1989 under Abulfaz Elchibey came out of the Baku intelligentsia.
keywords: Armenian National United Party of Paruyr Hayrikyan

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The shadow economy, the nuclear plant at Metsamor, the oil rocks and Sevan's rescue

entries.label: Oil Rocks and the Caspian
entries.hint: The offshore field and the town on piers of Neft Daşları (Oil Rocks), founded in 1949, extracted oil from the Caspian seabed to the end of the Soviet period, the first of its kind; Baku's production fell from the 1940s' peak as the Volga–Urals and Siberian fields rose, and Azerbaijan became a producer of machinery for oilfields.

entries.label: The second economy
entries.hint: The Caucasian republics, with warm climates and small private plots, grew citrus, tea, wine, flowers and vegetables for sale across the USSR and developed a large unofficial economy with its own networks, including corruption in the party and state; Shevardnadze and Aliyev, among others, made campaigns against it.
entries.note: Suny 1994; Gerald Mars and Yochanan Altman, studies of the Georgian second economy.

entries.label: Metsamor and the nuclear plant
entries.hint: The Armenian nuclear plant at Metsamor, with two VVER reactors of the first generation, began operation in 1976 and 1980; after the Spitak earthquake of 1988, the plant was shut down in early 1989 as a precaution and, in the energy crisis of the blockade, the government restarted a reactor in 1995.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Oil Rocks, the Arpa–Sevan tunnel, Metsamor and the Matenadaran

entries.label: The Arpa–Sevan tunnel
entries.hint: To save Lake Sevan, whose level had fallen by some 19 metres through its use for power and irrigation, the Soviets built from 1963 to 1981 a 48-kilometre tunnel to bring the water of the Arpa river to it, and in the 1980s began to stabilise and raise its level.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The diaspora's earthquake aid, the Nakhchivan border fence and the exodus of minorities

entries.label: The diaspora's earthquake aid
entries.hint: The earthquake of December 1988 brought help from some 100 countries, among them the US, Britain, France and also Turkey, whose aid planes crossed Armenian airspace; the Armenian diaspora and the Armenian General Benevolent Union sent funds, and the response was a first contact of Soviet Armenia with the diaspora in numbers.

entries.label: The Nakhchivan border fence
entries.hint: On 31 December 1989 tens of thousands of Azerbaijanis in Nakhchivan, with the Popular Front's call, tore down the border fences and crossed the Araxes to Iranian Azerbaijan, to meet their kin across the border; the date is now commemorated in Azerbaijan as a Day of Solidarity of Azerbaijanis of the World.
keywords: Day of Solidarity of Azerbaijanis of the World

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The Spitak earthquake, the Caspian's rise and the refugees

entries.label: The Spitak earthquake
entries.hint: An earthquake of magnitude 6.8 on 7 December 1988 destroyed Spitak and much of Leninakan (Gyumri), Kirovakan and villages in northern Armenia, killing, according to the official figure, some 25,000 people (some estimates are higher) and leaving about half a million homeless; prefabricated and poorly built buildings failed, and the disaster came at the height of the Karabakh crisis.
entries.note: Armenian Seismological Survey; Soviet government commission (1989); Suny 1993.

entries.label: The refugees of the conflicts
entries.hint: By 1991 the conflicts and expulsions in Karabakh and the border districts, the Meskhetian Turks' flight from Uzbekistan after the Fergana pogroms of 1989, and the dislocation of Georgians, Abkhaz and Ossetians had created several hundred thousand refugees and displaced persons in the three republics; the counts differ by source.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The women of 9 April, the refugees of 1988–1990 and the dissident prisoners

entries.label: The dissident prisoners
entries.hint: Georgians and Armenians were sent to camps and exile for petitions, samizdat journals and demonstrations: Gamsakhurdia and Kostava were sentenced in 1977 for human rights work and were pardoned in 1979 after recanting, the Armenian Hayrikyan spent years in the camps, and Parajanov was imprisoned for four years.

entries.label: The refugees of Sumgait and Baku
entries.hint: Armenians who fled Sumgait, Baku and Kirovabad, among them many elderly and families of mixed marriages, and the Azerbaijanis who left their villages in Armenia, were housed in hostels, tents and railway wagons, and a part of both groups were later displaced again by the war; the survivors' accounts are collected by human rights and oral history projects.
entries.note: Memorial, Helsinki Watch reports; de Waal 2003.

entries.label: The women of 9 April
entries.hint: Most of the 21 killed in Tbilisi on 9 April 1989 were young women, who had joined the hunger strike and rally outside the government house; their deaths, with some details of the sappers' spades and gas, became a national memory, and they are commemorated by name at the memorial at the site.
